newsitem.title: POLAND: Poles vote on controversial new constitution.
newsitem.headline: Poles vote on controversial new constitution.

text.p: Poles will decide in a referendum on Sunday either to adopt a new constitution sponsored by the ruling ex-communists or to stick with current makeshift arrangements in the hope of a better alternative in future.

The Solidarity union, which had a key role in toppling communism in 1989, wants voters to reject the constitution, saying it fails to reflect Poland's Christian heritage, guarantee sovereignty or settle past wrongs.
For the union and its rightist allies it is a harsh irony that ex-communists have been the main authors of a charter intended to entrench rights and liberties won by Solidarity eight years ago.
They are bitter that the referendum is happening so soon before general elections due in September in which the union-led Solidarity Election Action (AWS) alliance hopes to win power.
"To pass the constitution on the basis of a line-up that will change greatly in the next parliament is to place a time-bomb under Poland," said union leader Marian Krzaklewski.

In a last televised address late on Friday, before a 24-hour pre-vote ban on campaigning took effect, President Aleksander Kwasniewski urged compatriots to ignore political divisions and to back the new fundamental law.
"This is a good constitution, worthy of our past, allowing us to do justice to our national aspirations," said Kwasniewski, a former communist turned social-democrat.
Above all, Kwasniewski urged Poles to take part in the referendum.
But opinion polls suggest voters, baffled by the 243-article document and conflicting accounts from politicians about what it means, may stay away.
The vote will be binding no matter how low the turnout, but low participation would mean the heated debate will continue.
The draft is an unwieldy compromise reached between the ruling Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), its Peasant allies, and two liberal or leftist opposition parties in parliament.

It confirms civil rights, broadly keeps the current political system while weakening the presidency, sets caps on the government's spending but also obliges it to support employment and home-building.
Controversy has centred on visions of national identity.

Solidarity, seeing Poland's history as bound up with the majority Catholic faith, wanted the charter to clearly invoke God, place religious values above man-made law and include a clause effectively banning abortion -- now legal in Poland.
The bishops, greatly concerned over abortion, have announced deep moral reservations about the current document.

The right also says a section permitting Poland by treaty to surrender some functions to international organisations -- designed to ease its entry into the European structures -- unacceptably limits national sovereignty.
The constitution's authors, including leading opposition figure Tadeusz Mazowiecki, a Catholic and veteran democracy campaigner, reject these arguments as ill-founded or false.
Mazowiecki told Reuters the constitution was not perfect and he wished it had been drafted by a different parliament.
"But I don't expect a future parliament will be capable of such a compromise and I think Poland might not have such a parliament for a long time," Mazowiecki told Reuters.
That would leave Poland with the remains of the discredited 1952 constitution, amended by 1992 interim laws which do not lay down fundamental rights and liberties.
The charter's advocates say the constitution makes room for all, Catholics and people of other faiths or none -- and allows abortion laws to be tightened if the majority wishes.

Sociologists say that by appealing to Catholic sentiment, which may be boosted by the May 31-June 10 visit of Polish Pope John Paul, Solidarity risks narrowing its support in a country where many are formally Catholic but resent Church influence.
At present the AWS is rivalling the ex-communists for top place in opinion polls with about 25 percent each.
Mindful of past opinion surveys suggesting the new constitution will pass, Solidarity has been careful to say that this would not necessarily augur defeat in the election
